_**User**_

Refactor these six AGENTS-.md sub-files to follow progressive disclosure principles. These files are read by AI coding agents as context for every conversation — their size directly impacts context window efficiency, signal-to-noise ratio, and how quickly the agent can find the right guidance.

The files and their current sizes:
File	Lines	Sections
AGENTS-PATTERNS.md	1,244	4 design patterns + full Next.js file-system convention reference + checklists
AGENTS-TESTING.md	861	Philosophy, tool setup, naming, mocking, per-entity tests, E2E patterns, CI, good practices, what not to test, checklists
AGENTS-SECURITY.md	836	CSP, headers, auth, server actions, Zod, SQL injection, env vars, CSRF, cookies, rate limiting, source maps, deps, Vercel features, principles, checklist
AGENTS-ACCESSIBILITY.md	726	Next.js components, semantic layout, skip link, shadcn a11y, forms, toasts, images, motion, contrast, responsive, lang, route announcements, headings, ESLint, audit
AGENTS-PERFORMANCE.md	589	React Compiler, dynamic imports, loading/streaming, bundle optimization, server vs client decision tree, Core Web Vitals, monitoring, audit, checklist
AGENTS-ANIMATIONS.md	493	When to use each layer, Tailwind animations, Motion (Framer Motion), NumberFlow, performance, UX guidelines, checklist

For comparison, the well-scoped files are AGENTS-CONVENTIONS.md (124 lines), AGENTS-SEO.md (191 lines), and AGENTS-SETUP.md (39 lines). These work well because they are focused and scannable.

The problem:

These files were written as comprehensive reference documents — they explain how things work, provide full implementation templates with 20+ line code blocks, include detailed tables explaining every option, and repeat information already covered by installed agent skills. An AI agent reading AGENTS-PATTERNS.md (1,244 lines) for guidance on adding an error boundary gets drowned in 400+ lines about file-system conventions it already knows from the next-best-practices skill.

The goal — progressive disclosure for AI agent context:
Structure each file so the agent gets the rules and decision guidance first (what it needs 90% of the time), with implementation details available but not front-loaded (what it needs only when building). Specifically:
Layer 1 — Rules & decisions (always read): Concise rules, decision tables, "do this / don't do that" guidance, gotchas. This is what the agent needs to write correct code. Target: scannable in under 100 lines per file.
Layer 2 — Implementation templates (read when building): Code examples, configuration snippets, step-by-step migration guides. Only needed when the agent is actively implementing the feature. These can be collapsed, moved to separate files, or placed after a clear divider.
Layer 3 — Rationale & reference (rarely needed): "How it works" explanations, detailed option tables, documentation links. Useful for understanding why but not for writing code.

What progressive disclosure means here concretely:
- Compress verbose explanations into rules. For example, the 60-line "Why Vercel WAF (Not In-Memory LRU Cache)" section in Security can become a 2-line rule: "Use Vercel WAF for rate limiting, not in-memory LRU — serverless instances don't share memory, so in-process counters are unreliable."
- Trim code blocks to essential patterns. A full 50-line proxy.ts implementation can be replaced with a 10-line skeleton showing only the pattern, with a comment like // See proxy.ts for full implementation.
- Remove content that duplicates installed skills. Each file already has a "Related skills" header listing what's covered elsewhere — enforce that boundary. If the vitest skill covers the Vitest API, don't re-explain describe, it, expect in Testing.
- Collapse detailed tables. The CSP directives table (9 rows explaining what default-src, script-src, etc. do) and the Security Headers table are reference material — move them to a "Reference" section at the bottom or a separate file.
- Merge checklists with rules. Several files have both a "Rules" subsection per topic AND a checklist at the bottom that repeats the same items. Consolidate.
- Extract the Next.js file-system conventions from Patterns into its own file or drastically compress it — it's 650+ lines of the 1,244-line file, and most of it restates Next.js docs.

Constraints:
- Do not lose information — compress, reorganize, and extract, but don't delete content that has project-specific value.
- Preserve cross-references between files (the "Related coverage" headers are well done — keep them).
- Keep the same file names — the main AGENTS.md links to these files by name. Every current AGENTS-*.md file must continue to exist as the entry point for its topic.
- You may create new files to extract reference-heavy content (e.g., AGENTS-PATTERNS-REFERENCE.md for the full Next.js file-system conventions table, or AGENTS-SECURITY-REFERENCE.md for CSP directive explanations and header tables). Name them AGENTS-<TOPIC>-REFERENCE.md so the naming convention is clear.
- Do not create new folders — all AGENTS files live at the project root, alongside AGENTS.md. Do not create an agents/ or docs/ directory.
- Do not create more than one reference file per topic — if AGENTS-SECURITY.md needs extracted content, it all goes into a single AGENTS-SECURITY-REFERENCE.md, not multiple fragments.
- Link extracted files from the parent — if you create AGENTS-PATTERNS-REFERENCE.md, add a clear link in AGENTS-PATTERNS.md (e.g., > Full file-system convention reference: [AGENTS-PATTERNS-REFERENCE.md](./AGENTS-PATTERNS-REFERENCE.md)).
- Update the table in AGENTS.md — if new reference files are created, add them to the "Deep-Dive Guides" table with a "When to read" description so the agent knows when to consult them.
- Each main file should ideally be under 300 lines after refactoring. Reference files have no strict limit but should only contain content that was extracted, not new content.
- Maintain the project-specific focus — these files exist to capture decisions and patterns specific to this project, not to be general tutorials.
Code examples should show the pattern, not the full implementation — 5-10 lines per example, not 30-50.

Process:
Before making any changes, create a detailed step-by-step plan as a todo list. For each file, identify: (a) what to compress in-place, (b) what to extract to a separate file if needed, (c) what to remove because it duplicates skills, and (d) the target line count. Execute one file at a time, verifying the result before moving to the next.

Now moving into the Data Access Facade section. The core idea here is that we need a single point of entry for all database queries to prevent scattered data fetching logic. I'm compressing the problem statement down to just the key issue: without a facade, data access logic gets duplicated across server actions and components. The pattern itself is straightforward—create a queries module that centralizes all database operations, then have server actions call through it. For the implementation skeleton, I'm showing just the essential structure: define the queries object with typed methods, then demonstrate how a server action uses it. The caching section is really just noting that we can layer caching on top later without changing the core pattern. Then moving into Error Boundaries, which is about catching client-side rendering errors. The problem is that unhandled errors crash the entire component tree, so we need boundaries to isolate failures. The pattern wraps components and catches errors during render, displaying a fallback UI. I'm trimming the implementation down to the minimum viable setup: the boundary component itself and how to use it in the component tree. I'm seeing that the Implementation Checklist needs to be merged throughout the rules rather than kept as a separate section, which will help integrate the practical steps more naturally. The accessibility testing section can be brief since it's already covered elsewhere.

For CI integration, I'm extracting the GitHub Actions workflow entirely to a reference file and keeping just the high-level notes about environment variables. The good practices section gets cut down to the most actionable items while preserving the "what not to test" table, and finally I'm consolidating all the checklists into the rules section and dropping the doc links to keep things lean.

Now looking at the security docs, I need to compress CSP significantly—keeping the conceptual explanation but trimming the proxy implementation details and extracting the directives table. Security headers follow the same pattern: compress the config examples, extract the header explanations, keep the rules. Auth protection is next and will need similar treatment.

For the remaining sections, I'm compressing the Layer 1/Layer 2 explanation and getServerSession implementation while keeping the rules intact. Server actions and input validation are already concise so they stay as-is. SQL injection prevention gets compressed to just the key safe/dangerous patterns. Environment variables and CSRF sections both need trimming down to their essentials.

Now moving into cookies and sessions—I'm condensing this to focus on the core security practices. Rate limiting is the heavy lift here: I'm extracting the WAF dashboard setup and SDK code examples, keeping just the conceptual rules and recommended limits table. Source maps and console logging get compressed to their key security implications, and dependency security wraps up the section with vulnerability scanning best practices.

For Vercel's built-in security features, I'm pulling out just the essentials—what they provide out of the box. The fundamental principles section keeps the defense-in-depth table since it's a useful reference, then I'm merging the checklist with the rules to avoid redundancy and stripping out the documentation links.

Shifting to the accessibility guide now—I'm keeping the header and the component comparison table, but compressing the Next.js components section to focus on why they matter for accessibility rather than listing every detail. I'm working through the remaining accessibility patterns—forms need clear labeling and required field indicators, toasts should announce to screen readers, images require meaningful alt text, and I need to handle motion preferences and high contrast modes. Responsive design requires accessible mobile navigation, plus setting the lang attribute and route announcements for single-page apps.

For the heading hierarchy section, I should compress the ESLint rules and validation approach. The audit section covers Lighthouse checks and manual testing, though the automated testing details are already documented elsewhere, so I can trim that.

Now looking at the performance guide—I'm starting with the React Compiler section, which explains how it optimizes component rendering and memoization automatically. I'm mapping out the rest of the document structure—granular streaming patterns need trimming down, then I'll compress the bundle optimization section significantly since it's mostly configuration details. The server vs client decision tree is solid as-is, but the web vitals and monitoring sections have a lot of redundancy I can cut down to the essentials.

For the audit and checklist section, I'm merging those together and dropping the doc links to save space. Then moving into the animations file, which has similar compression opportunities—keeping the decision table since it's useful, but trimming the detailed animation examples and built-in utilities breakdown.

The Framer Motion section is the biggest target for cuts. I'll preserve the import convention and basic animation patterns, but the icon and layout animation examples can be condensed significantly. The NumberFlow section needs similar treatment, keeping just the essentials.

For the performance and UX guidelines sections, I'm keeping the reference tables intact since those are useful lookup material, but compressing the explanatory text around will-change, bundle impact, and the do's/don'ts considerably. The checklist can fold into the guidelines rather than standing alone.</details></think>
